firmware.build_command: source ~/export-esp.sh && cargo +esp build --target xtensa-esp32s3-none-elf --bin llm-limit-bench --release -Z build-std=core,alloc

paths_compared.exact_f32: stores f32 keys/values and scores f32 keys directly
paths_compared.int4_decode_score: stores packed int4 keys/values, dequantizes key elements while scoring, dequantizes values for aggregation
paths_compared.compressed_score: stores packed int4 keys/values, quantizes query once and scores packed int4 key nibbles directly, dequantizes values for aggregation

interpretation.capacity_result: int4 KV gives 8x theoretical KV capacity versus exact f32 for this model shape
interpretation.speed_result: compressed-score path was slightly slower than int4 decode-score in this pure-Rust hardware run (21.33 tok/s vs 21.70 tok/s, 0.98x)
interpretation.claim_boundary: This is a no_std ESP32-S3 compressed-key scoring gate on deterministic fixture transformer weights. It is not a trained checkpoint quality result and not a full fib-quant/turbo-quant Gram-table port.
interpretation.next_gate: Use ESP-NN/SIMD or a real no_std fib/turbo compressed-domain scorer; current scalar query quantization overhead offsets packed-key scoring savings.

blockers: Compressed-score implementation still decodes values for aggregation; only key scoring changed.
Pure Rust scalar int4 packed scoring did not improve speed on ESP32-S3; compressed-domain math needs SIMD/Gram-table style implementation to become a speed win.
Fixture transformer weights measure engine envelope, not language quality.
